lede: A model in Spark is one more pipeline stage: you fit it on training rows, and the fitted pipeline turns new rows into predictions. Knowing which objects learn and which only apply, how to keep a fitted pipeline, and how to measure it on rows it never saw is what makes the predictions worth trusting.
objectives: Tell estimators, transformers and models apart, and fit a `Pipeline` that ends in `LinearRegression` or `LogisticRegression`
Read predictions and probabilities from a fitted model, and save and load a `PipelineModel`
Split data into training and test rows the same way on every run, by a hash of the key instead of `randomSplit`
Measure a model with `RegressionEvaluator` and `BinaryClassificationEvaluator`, rounding metrics before comparing them

blocks.md:
Feature preparation used two kinds of objects. An **estimator** has `fit(df)`: it learns from the data and returns a **model**. A **transformer** has `transform(df)`: it adds columns and keeps the rest. Every model is a transformer.

A machine-learning algorithm is just another estimator. `LinearRegression` reads a vector column (`featuresCol`, by default `features`) and a number column to predict (`labelCol`, by default `label`). `fit` returns a `LinearRegressionModel`, whose `transform` adds a `prediction` column.

`movies` has one row per film, with its `release_year` and `runtime_min`. Can the year predict the length?

blocks.title: An estimator fits, its model transforms
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.regression import LinearRegression

films = VectorAssembler(inputCols=["release_year"], outputCol="features").transform(movies)

lr = LinearRegression(labelCol="runtime_min")
model = lr.fit(films)
print(type(lr).__name__, "->", type(model).__name__)
print(round(model.coefficients[0], 3), round(model.intercept, 1))

model.transform(films).select(
    "movie_id", "release_year", "runtime_min", F.round("prediction", 1).alias("prediction")
).orderBy("movie_id").show()
blocks.note: The fitted line loses about 1.8 minutes per release year. Films from the same year all get the same prediction, and many are far from their real runtime: the year alone tells you little. The coefficients are rounded because the last digits of a fitted number can change when the data is split into partitions differently.

blocks.md: Even with one input, the model wants a **vector**. Passing the plain column is the most common first mistake.

blocks.title: A number column is not a features vector
blocks.note: The message says the column must be of type `VectorUDT` but was `int`. Put a `VectorAssembler` in front of the model, even for a single column.

blocks.md:
In a `Pipeline`, the model is the last stage. `pipeline.fit(train)` fits each estimator in turn on the output of the stages before it, and returns a `PipelineModel` whose stages are all transformers. `model.stages[-1]` is the fitted model itself, with its coefficients.

`LogisticRegression` predicts a yes/no label: 1.0 or 0.0. Its model adds three columns: `rawPrediction`, `probability` (a vector with the chance of 0.0, then of 1.0) and `prediction`, which is 1.0 when the chance of 1.0 is above one half.

Below, a small table of film features, as a `groupBy` over ratings would produce: each film's average rating in one year, and a label saying whether it stayed at 4.0 or more the next year.

blocks.title: A pipeline that ends in a model
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.functions import vector_to_array

films = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("M01", 4.5, 1.0), ("M02", 4.0, 1.0), ("M03", 3.5, 0.0), ("M04", 3.0, 0.0), ("M05", 2.5, 0.0),
     ("M06", 4.5, 0.0), ("M07", 3.5, 1.0), ("M08", 1.5, 0.0), ("M09", 4.0, 1.0), ("M10", 5.0, 1.0)],
    "movie_id STRING, avg_rating DOUBLE, label DOUBLE",
)

pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[
    VectorAssembler(inputCols=["avg_rating"], outputCol="features"),
    LogisticRegression(),
])
model = pipeline.fit(films)
print([type(s).__name__ for s in pipeline.getStages()])
print([type(s).__name__ for s in model.stages])

lr = model.stages[-1]
print(round(float(lr.coefficients[0]), 2), round(lr.intercept, 2))

scored = model.transform(films)
print(scored.columns)
scored.select(
    "movie_id", "avg_rating", "label",
    F.round(vector_to_array("probability")[1], 2).alias("p_high"),
    "prediction",
).orderBy("movie_id").show()
blocks.note: The pipeline held a `LogisticRegression`; the fitted pipeline holds a `LogisticRegressionModel`. A higher average gives a higher chance, so films with the same average get the same `p_high`. M06 and M07 are predicted wrong: the model draws one line, and those films don't follow it.

blocks.md:
Fitting can take a while on real data, and the rows you score later arrive in another job. `model.write().overwrite().save(path)` writes the fitted pipeline to a folder: its settings as JSON in `metadata`, each fitted stage under `stages`. `PipelineModel.load(path)` reads it back, ready to `transform`, with nothing fitted again. Here the folder is under `/tmp`, private to this run.

An **evaluator** turns predictions into one number. `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` reads `label` and `rawPrediction` and by default gives the **area under the ROC curve**: 1.0 when every film labelled 1.0 is ranked above every film labelled 0.0, 0.5 for a coin toss.

blocks.title: Save the fitted pipeline, load it back
blocks.code:
import os
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline, PipelineModel
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

films = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("M01", 4.5, 1.0), ("M02", 4.0, 1.0), ("M03", 3.5, 0.0), ("M04", 3.0, 0.0), ("M05", 2.5, 0.0),
     ("M06", 4.5, 0.0), ("M07", 3.5, 1.0), ("M08", 1.5, 0.0), ("M09", 4.0, 1.0), ("M10", 5.0, 1.0)],
    "movie_id STRING, avg_rating DOUBLE, label DOUBLE",
)
model = Pipeline(stages=[
    VectorAssembler(inputCols=["avg_rating"], outputCol="features"),
    LogisticRegression(),
]).fit(films)

model.write().overwrite().save("/tmp/film_model")
print(sorted(os.listdir("/tmp/film_model")))

loaded = PipelineModel.load("/tmp/film_model")
print([type(s).__name__ for s in loaded.stages])

before = model.transform(films).select("movie_id", "probability").collect()
after = loaded.transform(films).select("movie_id", "probability").collect()
print(before == after)

auc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator().evaluate(loaded.transform(films))
print(round(auc, 3))
blocks.note: The loaded pipeline gives exactly the same probabilities. The area under the curve is 0.84: mostly well ranked, with the two films that break the pattern pulling it below 1.0. It is measured on the rows the model was fitted on, which flatters it.

blocks.md:
To measure honestly, hold some rows back: fit on the **training** rows and evaluate on the **test** rows.

`df.randomSplit([0.7, 0.3], seed=7)` draws rows at random. The seed makes it repeat on the same data **with the same partitions**, because each partition draws its own random numbers. Read the same rows into a different number of partitions and other rows land in the test set. That happens whenever an upstream step, a file layout or a cluster size changes.

A split by a **hash of the key** doesn't depend on partitions at all. `F.crc32("movie_id")` turns the id into a whole number that is always the same for the same id, so `F.crc32("movie_id") % 3 == 0` puts about a third of the films in the test set, and always the same ones.

blocks.title: A random split moves with the partitions
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    train, test = movies.repartition(n).randomSplit([0.7, 0.3], seed=7)
    print(n, "partitions:", sorted(r.movie_id for r in test.collect()))

for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    test = movies.repartition(n).filter(F.crc32("movie_id") % 3 == 0)
    print(n, "partitions:", sorted(r.movie_id for r in test.collect()))
blocks.note: Same seed, three different test sets. The hash split picks M01, M03, M06, M07 and M08 every time. Choose the key the rows belong to: split films by `movie_id` so no film is in both sets.

blocks.md:
`RegressionEvaluator` compares `label` (or your `labelCol`) with `prediction`. Its default metric is `rmse`, the root mean squared error, in the label's units: minutes here. Ask for another metric with `metricName`, or pass `{evaluator.metricName: "mae"}` to `evaluate` for one call.

Round metrics before you print or compare them. The last digits can change with the partitioning, while the first few don't.

blocks.title: Measure on films the model never saw
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.regression import LinearRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import RegressionEvaluator

films = VectorAssembler(inputCols=["release_year"], outputCol="features").transform(movies)
held_out = F.crc32("movie_id") % 3 == 0
train, test = films.filter(~held_out), films.filter(held_out)

model = LinearRegression(labelCol="runtime_min").fit(train)
evaluator = RegressionEvaluator(labelCol="runtime_min")

print("train rmse", round(evaluator.evaluate(model.transform(train)), 2))
print("test rmse", round(evaluator.evaluate(model.transform(test)), 2))
print("test mae", round(evaluator.evaluate(model.transform(test), {evaluator.metricName: "mae"}), 2))
blocks.note: The error on the five held-out films is almost three times the error on the training films. On training rows a model is marked on its own homework.

blocks.md: Choosing settings, such as `regParam` (how strongly the coefficients are held towards zero), is the same idea repeated. `ParamGridBuilder` lists the settings to try. `CrossValidator` splits the rows into `numFolds` folds, fits the estimator (a model or a whole pipeline) on all but one fold and scores the one left out, for every setting, and keeps the best average. Its folds are drawn at random with a `seed`, so like `randomSplit` it repeats only on the same data in the same partitions.

blocks.title: Try settings with CrossValidator
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.regression import LinearRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import RegressionEvaluator
from pyspark.ml.tuning import CrossValidator, ParamGridBuilder

films = VectorAssembler(inputCols=["release_year"], outputCol="features").transform(movies)
films = films.withColumn("label", F.col("runtime_min").cast("double"))

lr = LinearRegression()
grid = ParamGridBuilder().addGrid(lr.regParam, [0.0, 100.0]).build()
cv = CrossValidator(estimator=lr, estimatorParamMaps=grid, evaluator=RegressionEvaluator(), numFolds=2, seed=7)
result = cv.fit(films)

print([round(float(m), 2) for m in result.avgMetrics])
print(result.bestModel.getRegParam())
blocks.note: One average RMSE per setting, in grid order. RMSE is better when lower, and the evaluator knows it, so the strong setting wins here: with a year that predicts little, holding the line flat does better. `bestModel` is the model refitted on all rows with the winning setting. Every setting is fitted once per fold, so a grid gets expensive fast.

choices: A `LogisticRegressionModel`, a transformer that adds predictions
The training DataFrame with a `prediction` column
The pipeline's area under the ROC curve
concept.why: Fitting a pipeline replaces every estimator with the model it fitted. The last stage is the fitted `LogisticRegressionModel`, which `transform` uses to add `rawPrediction`, `probability` and `prediction`.

concept.prompt: A job splits its rows with `randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)`. After an upstream change, the same rows arrive in more partitions. What happens to the test set?
choices: It stays the same, because the seed is fixed
It can contain different rows, because each partition draws its own random numbers
Spark raises an error about the partitions
concept.why: The seed repeats the split only for the same data in the same partitions. A split by a hash of the key, such as `F.crc32("movie_id") % 5 == 0`, puts the same rows in the test set whatever the partitioning.

concept.prompt: A runtime model has an RMSE of 7 minutes on its training films and 19 on held-out films. Which number tells you how it will do on new films?
choices: 7, because it was measured on more films
19, because those films played no part in fitting
Neither: RMSE only works on training rows
concept.why: A model fits its training rows as closely as it can, so their error is too optimistic. Rows held out of fitting stand in for new data.

review: An estimator's `fit` returns a model; a model is a transformer whose `transform` adds columns. Algorithms like `LinearRegression` are estimators too.
Models read one vector column, `features` by default, and a `label`: put a `VectorAssembler` in front even for one input.
A fitted `Pipeline` is a `PipelineModel`; `stages[-1]` is the fitted model. `write().overwrite().save(path)` and `PipelineModel.load(path)` keep it for later jobs.
`LogisticRegression` adds `probability` (chance of 0.0, then 1.0) and `prediction`; `vector_to_array("probability")[1]` is the chance of 1.0.
`randomSplit` with a seed repeats only on the same partitions. Split by a hash of the key, like `F.crc32("movie_id") % 3 == 0`, to get the same test rows every run.
Measure on held-out rows with `RegressionEvaluator` or `BinaryClassificationEvaluator`, and round coefficients and metrics: their last digits can vary.
